heading: Binary search on the answer
body:
Not searching **in** the array—searching **for** the answer.

**The trick:** Your search space is `[1, max(piles)]` (all possible speeds), not the piles themselves.

**Why it works:** If speed `k` finishes in time, any speed `k' > k` also works. This monotonic property creates a sorted T/F array `[F, F, F, T, T, T]`—perfect for binary search to find the **minimum valid** speed.

heading: The ceiling-division gotcha
body:
For each pile, hours needed = `ceil(pile / speed)`.

**Don't use:** `math.ceil(pile / speed)` (floating point can cause precision errors)

**Do use:** `(pile + speed - 1) // speed` (pure integer math)

Example: pile=7, speed=3 → `(7+2)//3 = 3` hours ✓

label: Crux · Python

q: Why is the feasibility function monotonic in this problem?
options: Because the piles array is sorted in increasing order
Because if speed k works, any speed k' > k also works (eating faster never makes it take longer)
Because we use ceiling division when calculating hours needed
Because the maximum speed is always max(piles)
explain: Eating faster never makes things worse—if speed k works, any k' > k also works, creating [F,F,F,T,T,T].
